opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think order matters enormously, and it's something we don't talk about nearly enough. When you look at how a person comes to understand the world, there's a real developmental sequence. You learn about objects, about symmetry, about cause and effect, and only later do you layer more abstract concepts on top of that foundation. Each new idea gets built on the scaffolding of what came before, and that tends to produce what I'd call a well-organized, or unified, representation. The pieces fit together in a way that reflects the actual structure of the world.

With LLMs it's quite different. Everything gets thrown at them more or less at once. You've got calculus sitting next to children's stories sitting next to legal documents, all shuffled together, and the objective is just to get the next token right. There's no sense of "first understand this, then build that." So the network can find ways to get the answers right that don't reflect any deep regularity. It can arrive at the right output through a kind of patchwork.

This connects to some work we did looking at Picbreeder images, where people evolved images through open-ended exploration. When you look inside those networks, the representations are remarkably elegant. If there's a symmetric face, there's literally a component encoding symmetry, and you can vary one thing, like how wide the mouth opens, and it changes in a sensible way. Then if you train a network with conventional SGD to produce exactly the same image, the output looks identical, but the internals are a mess. That's what we've been calling fractured, entangled representation. Same behavior on the surface, completely different underneath.

And I think the key difference there was the path. In Picbreeder, the images were discovered incrementally, stepping stone by stepping stone, where people weren't even aiming at the final image. Each step had its own coherence, so the representation accumulated in an orderly way. SGD goes straight for the target, and the result is something that works but isn't really organized around the underlying concepts.

Why does that matter if the output is the same? Because representation determines what you can do next. If you want creativity, continual learning, generalization to something genuinely new, you need the representation to be organized in a way that makes the next good idea nearby. A fractured representation might give you the right answer on the benchmark, but it's a poor springboard for invention. So when people ask why these models are so impressive yet sometimes strangely brittle, I suspect part of the answer is that the order of learning, the absence of a sensible developmental path, leaves the internals much messier than the behavior would suggest.

r001.rationale: The response describes humans learning foundational ideas before layering on abstractions, producing an orderly, unified representation.

r002.rationale: It says LLMs learn from mixed material without a developmental sequence, but does not say children ignore material beyond their readiness.

r003.rationale: Calculus is mentioned only as an example of mixed LLM training material; the response does not discuss learning it before arithmetic or constructing heuristic arithmetic.

r004.rationale: The response discusses fractured, entangled representations, but does not attribute multiple representations of a concept to learning advanced material before its prerequisites.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think order is actually the whole story, and it's one of the most underappreciated things about why these systems end up with the kind of representations they have.

So think about how a human learns. You don't get everything at once. You get a trickle, and that trickle is structured by the fact that you're embodied, you have limited attention, you can only engage with one thing at a time. And crucially, you're not really trying to learn, you're trying to understand. A kid doesn't learn language by predicting the next word in a corpus. They learn "ball" because they want the ball. The concept gets grounded in something that matters to them, and then subsequent concepts get built on top of that one, and the scaffolding that results is a kind of hierarchy where every piece is sitting on top of something that was already understood. The order imposes a decomposition. Each thing you learn has to be compatible with everything that came before, and that forces the representation to be modular, to have clean parts, because you literally can't hold a messy tangled version of it and still learn the next thing.

Now contrast that with how we train an LLM. You take the entire internet, shuffle it, and present it in essentially random order, and you ask the network to minimize loss over all of it simultaneously. There's no reason for it to build up a structured scaffold, because it's never in a position where understanding one thing well is a prerequisite for the next thing. Everything is being optimized at once. And what you get, I would argue, is something I've called fractured entangled representation. The network does find a solution, and the solution works in the sense that it produces the right outputs, but internally it's this spaghetti where the same concept is represented in several different places that don't know about each other, and unrelated concepts are sharing the same weights in ways that make no sense if you look at them.

The experiment that really made this concrete for me was comparing networks that were evolved through something like Picbreeder, where humans picked images step by step, one at a time, in a sequence where each step built on the last, versus networks trained by SGD to produce the exact same final image. Same output. Pixel for pixel. But if you look inside, the Picbreeder network has this beautiful decomposition, you can find the single weight that controls symmetry or the mouth opening, and the SGD network has nothing like that. You can't find anything. And the only difference is the order in which the thing was discovered. The human-guided one went through a sequence of stepping stones, each of which was itself a coherent thing, and the representation inherited that coherence.

So I think when people talk about LLMs having impressive capabilities but weird failure modes, poor generalization, difficulty with continual learning, hallucination in strange places, I suspect a lot of that traces back to the representation, and the representation traces back to the fact that nothing was learned in order. It's not that these systems are too small or haven't seen enough data. It's that they were never forced to build understanding on understanding. And I don't think you fix that with more scale. I think you fix it by taking seriously that the path matters, not just the destination.

r001.rationale: It says human learning proceeds in a structured sequence, with each concept built on what was already understood, creating a coherent scaffold.

r002.rationale: It contrasts gradual, limited human learning with LLMs training on shuffled internet data, but does not say children ignore material they are not ready for.

r003.rationale: It does not mention learning calculus before arithmetic or constructing a heuristic version of arithmetic.

r004.rationale: It says LLM representations can place the same concept in several disconnected locations, but does not connect this to learning advanced material before its prerequisites.

astra-6.text:
I think the order matters a lot, because what you already know determines what you can make of the next thing you encounter. Learning isn’t just accumulating facts. It changes the way you interpret subsequent experience. So even if two learners encounter the same information, encountering it in a different order could lead them to different representations.

For humans, there’s this interesting asymmetry: we have a lot of experience with the world before we can describe it in language. We’re seeing things, moving around, discovering that our actions have consequences. Then language comes along and connects to that existing foundation. With a language model, at least in the text-first case, you’re starting with descriptions. There’s an enormous amount of structure in those descriptions, but it’s a different route into understanding.

What I find interesting is whether those routes eventually converge. If you give a language model perception and action later, does it arrive at something like the representations we have? Or does its earlier learning make it interpret those experiences in a fundamentally different way? I don’t think we should assume either answer.

This connects to the idea of stepping stones. An early discovery opens up possibilities that weren’t accessible before, and those possibilities influence what can be discovered next. The history of learning may be part of the explanation for the intelligence you end up with, rather than just a detail about how you got there.

r001.rationale: The response says human experience precedes language, but does not claim humans naturally learn in an order conducive to building good representations.

r002.rationale: It contrasts humans’ world experience with text-first models, but does not say children ignore material beyond their readiness or that LLMs learn from whatever material they are given.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention calculus, arithmetic, or advanced learning forcing a heuristic version of a prerequisite.

r004.rationale: It discusses learning histories shaping representations, but does not suggest that prerequisite gaps produce multiple separate representations of one concept.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the order matters a great deal, because what you already know determines how you interpret the next thing you encounter. Learning isn’t just accumulating facts in a bucket. Each new experience comes into a system that already has some structure, and that structure makes certain distinctions easier to see than others.

For humans, language comes into a life that’s already underway. We’ve been seeing things, moving around, wanting things, discovering that our actions have consequences. So when we learn a word, it can connect to this whole foundation of experience. With an LLM, you can start with language and build up an enormous amount of structure from relationships within language itself. That’s a very different route, even if eventually the two systems can give similar answers to a question.

What interests me is whether those routes lead to different possibilities for what gets learned next. You might think that if you expose a system to enough information, it will eventually all wash out and you’ll get the same representation. But I don’t think we should assume that. A concept you acquire early can become a stepping stone that makes some later concept accessible. If you encounter those things in the opposite order, you may never make that connection, or you may make a completely different one.

So there’s a developmental question here that goes beyond how much data you have. What sequence of experiences makes a particular kind of understanding possible? And there may be many different sequences that produce intelligence, without producing the same kind of intelligence.

r001.rationale: The response says humans encounter language after other experiences and that prior structure shapes learning, but it does not claim humans naturally learn in an order conducive to building good representations.

r002.rationale: It does not describe children ignoring material they are not ready for or contrast that with LLMs learning from any material provided.

r003.rationale: It does not mention calculus before arithmetic or a learner constructing a heuristic version of arithmetic.

r004.rationale: It allows that learning in a different order may lead to different connections, but does not say advanced material before prerequisites produces multiple separate representations of one concept.
